name: Diego Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No problem. Fire away, I like a chat.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Great. Could you walk me through a normal working day, start to finish?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I pick at a car parts distribution warehouse on the trading estate, the one that supplies garages across the county. Brake pads, oil filters, wiper blades, the odd exhaust. Garages order in the morning and want the part by lunch, so it's fast, scan, bag, label, onto the van shelf for the next run. Eight till five, and Saturday mornings every other week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the speed, and I like knowing the parts, I can tell a Ford pad from a Vauxhall one by feel now. What wears me out is the pay, it's low for what we do, and I share a flat with my brother Lars to make the rent work. I've got less than a month saved because I spent my savings on a van I'm doing up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, the hype was overdone. I use AI every day, it's useful, but it's a tool, not a miracle. At work I'd say keep your head down and keep earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I carry on with my plan. I'm doing up an old van to start a little parts delivery round on the side, for the small garages the big depot doesn't bother with. AI helps me plan the route and do the sums, but the work is mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the warehouse job full time while I finish the van, probably three more months. Then I'd start Saturday runs for two or three garages I know. I'd put every spare penny into the van insurance and a proper sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money, but I like where I'm going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that a risk with less than a month saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it is. If the van breaks I've got nothing. But I'd rather risk a bit now while it's just me and my brother than when I've got a wife and kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad says go for it, he ran his own window cleaning round for years. My mum worries. Lars says he'll drive for me if I get busy.

steps.text: Finish doing up the old van in three months
Run Saturday parts deliveries for small garages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people who are willing to work. Small businesses can do more with less. I'd say it at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the ordering side at the depot goes to software, the people who take garage calls. The picking will stay a while, parts are fiddly. My round might actually benefit, because small garages will order through apps and want quick drop-offs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the warehouse job and start my round. I'd use AI to build a simple ordering page for my garages, so they message me and I deliver. I'd aim for £400 a month extra by the end of the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited. It's my kind of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The girls on the phones, there are four of them. They know the garages better than anyone. I'd tell them to come and work with me if the round grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big depot could start its own fast delivery and undercut me. That's the risk. But they're slow, they're a big company.

steps.text: Launch the parts delivery round for small garages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shake-up, and people need to get moving. I'd say don't wait for the government. Start something, learn something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the picking goes by 2031 and probably the vans drive themselves not long after. My round has maybe three or four good years. And the garages themselves change, if cars fix themselves less and robots fix them more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the round hard in the first year, get it to full time if I can. I'd save £100 a month, which is hard on my pay. And I'd look at what else garages will need, like electric car parts or tyre storage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a fighting way. I'd feel the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three years before the robots are my window. Three years of hands-on work the robots can't do yet. I'd grab every bit of it, evenings, Saturdays, the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Going out, the gym, the second phone. I'd keep the van and the insurance, that's the business.

say: I'd say it's a **shake-up** and people need to get moving.
I'd tell people **don't wait** for the government: start something.
think: Picking goes by **2031**, and self-driving vans may follow soon after.
My round has maybe **three or four** good years.
do: Push the **round to full time** in the first year.
Save **£100 a month**, which is hard on his pay.
Look at what garages will need, like **electric car parts**.
feel: **Anxious** in a fighting way, feeling the clock.
S2.quote: The three years before the robots are my window. Three years of hands-on work the robots can't do yet.
fieldNote: Treats the **three-year gap** as a window to grab.
He sees that his own delivery round has a **shelf life** too, once vans drive themselves.

steps.text: Grow the parts delivery round to full time
Save £100 a month from the depot wage
Cut the gym, nights out and the second phone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good run-up, so build something now instead of moaning. I'd post about my round as an example, photos of the van, the garages I serve. Somebody my age might see it and think, I could do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years to AGI, eight to robots. I'd be 35. That's enough to have a proper small business, maybe two vans and Lars driving one. Then I'd need to change again, but I'd have savings by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the round this year and go full time in year two, once I've got eight garages regular. I'd buy a second van in year three if it's working, a cheap one from the auctions. And I'd use AI for the bookings, invoices and routes from day one, so I'm not up till midnight doing paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more hopeful. It's long enough to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if it doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I go back to picking or driving for someone, and I'd be no worse than my mates. I'd have tried, which matters to me. My dad always says nobody remembers the man who played it safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, local lads, maybe the phone girls from the depot, because they know every garage by name. I'd rather give jobs than take them.

think: At **35** I could have two vans with my brother driving one.
Then I'd need to **change again**, but with savings.

S3.quote: I'd rather give jobs than take them.
fieldNote: He wants to **hire locals**, including depot phone staff.

steps.text: Go full time on the delivery round in year two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so get building. I'd tell my mates at work to start side things now, a van, a stall, anything. Online I'd say the same, nobody's coming to save you, but that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots 2039, I'd be 40. I'd have a proper business by then, maybe more than vans, maybe a small parts shop of my own. I feel good about that, honestly. The only thing that would sink me is something going wrong this year before I've got a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the round and grow it slowly, one garage at a time. I'd save £50 a month before buying anything else for the van. And I'd keep the warehouse job till the round pays more, no jumping early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly the money right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The van breaking with no savings, honestly. The gearbox is original and it's done 180,000 miles. That's this year's worry, not 2039's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger self?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save before you buy the van. I did it backwards. I'd still buy it, mind, just a year later.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my round only gets a few good years. What would help is cheap small business loans and less paperwork for starting up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about people who want to build something. Everyone talks about losing jobs, but some of us want to make them. That needs a bit of help too.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about losing jobs, but some of us want to make them.
portrait: **Diego** is 27 and picks car parts at a depot supplying garages, sharing a flat with his brother.
He spent his savings on an old **van** to start a parts delivery round.
He's **traditional** on family, free-market on work, and uses AI daily.
He sees AI as a **chance** for small businesses and wants to hire locals.
He stays uneasy to **anxious**, treating the robot gap as a window.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his delivery round gets only a few good years.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **small business loans** and less **paperwork** for starting up.
